title: Rolling rotis
hook: kneading and rolling bread in the langar is seva with dough

segments.voice: Yesterday, the langar's open door, for anyone, no questions asked. Your line was the door stays open. Did you notice someone who could use a meal? Day one hundred sixteen.
screen: `THE KITCHEN DOOR STAYS OPEN — THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Walk into the back of a busy gurdwara kitchen on a Sunday morning and follow the smell of flour and hot iron. Around a low table, a circle of women and men sit on the floor with rolling pins. One pinches off balls of dough. The next flattens them. The next rolls them into circles, turning them with a little flick after every push. Nearby, someone flips them on a huge, flat iron griddle, then onto the open flame for a second, where they puff up like small balloons. Flour on everyone's arms. Gossip, laughter, a shabad playing on someone's phone. And a stack of rotis growing taller by the minute.
screen: `FLOUR AND HOT IRON.` → `PINCH, FLATTEN, ROLL, FLIP.` → `A STACK GROWING TALLER.`

segments.voice: Roti is the simple flatbread at the center of a Punjabi meal, and it's at the center of langar too. In many gurdwaras the rotis in langar are called prashada, the same word used for something received as a blessing. That tells you how the bread is seen. It's not just food. It's something given. Rolling rotis is seva with dough. It uses all three of the sevas you met: the hands knead and roll, the mind teaches the new person how to turn the circle, and the flour itself is often bought with daswandh. It's also one of the best places in the gurdwara to learn. Grandmothers teach teenagers. Beginners make lopsided shapes, and nobody minds, because a lopsided roti tastes the same. In the biggest kitchens, like the Harmandir Sahib's, machines now help make thousands of rotis an hour, but volunteers still roll by hand beside them. Think back to the bread in the stories. On day thirty-three, Guru Nanak chose the coarse bread of Bhai Lalo, a carpenter who earned it honestly, over the rich feast of a man who didn't. On day forty-six, Mata Khivi ran the kitchen at Khadur, and tradition remembers her langar for its care and its warmth. Bread in Sikh stories is never just bread. It carries the honesty of whoever earned it, and the love of whoever made it. So when you roll a roti in langar, you're adding yourself to a long line: Lalo, Khivi, and every volunteer since. Round, warm, and shared.
screen: `ROTI, CALLED PRASHADA IN LANGAR.` · `ALL THREE SEVAS IN ONE BREAD.` · `LOPSIDED TASTES THE SAME.` · `LALO'S BREAD, KHIVI'S KITCHEN.` · then, large: `ROUND, WARM, SHARED.`

segments.voice: If you have bread nearby, a roti, a slice, a cracker, hold it in your hands. If not, picture one, warm from the pan. Think of the people behind it: whoever grew the wheat, milled the flour, mixed the dough, baked it, drove it, sold it. Hundreds of hands. Then think of one person you could share bread with this week. See yourself tearing it in two, and handing them the bigger half. The bell holds the time.
Rolling rotis. The seva of making langar's bread by hand, called prashada in many gurdwaras: something given, not just food.
Your line: round, warm, shared. Today, make or buy some bread, and share it with someone, with the bigger half going to them. Day one hundred sixteen.

screen: `DAY 116 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MEAL EVERYONE CAN EAT.`

howItsDone: Volunteers in gurdwara kitchens knead, roll and cook rotis for langar, often sitting together on the floor; newcomers are welcome to learn, and in the largest kitchens machines help alongside hand-rolling.
